project_name: BioValue AI demo: fictional softwood kraft lignin stream
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: The stream leaves the mill as wet cake and no lignin dryer is available, so buyers needing dry powder would need to provide drying.
The lignin is currently fired in the mill's boilers as internal fuel, so external sale would compete with that use.
Solvent or membrane fractionation is not available, limiting pathways that require fractionated lignin.
Chemical modification equipment is not available, limiting pathways that require modified lignin.
Moisture is uncertain and affects dry tonnage and the mass that must be shipped.
Ash is missing, and sodium is missing, so inorganic-content requirements cannot be fully assessed.
data_quality_notes: The record is fictional demo data; all figures are illustrative assumptions rather than measurements from a real mill.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, ash, and sodium are missing.
The lignin-content analytical method is unclear and stated for illustration only.
Moisture is uncertain; production and quality are assumed to vary over the year.
The profile must be replaced with the mill's own laboratory data and production records before decisions are made.
agent.summary: Validated fictional softwood kraft lignin filter-cake profile: the recorded dry-matter balance passes, but composition is incomplete and the stream remains constrained by wet handling, unavailable processing equipment, and its current internal-fuel use.

lignin_pct.method: Acid-insoluble (Klason) plus acid-soluble lignin, as % of dry matter (method stated for illustration)

sulfur_pct.method: Total sulfur by elemental analysis (stated for illustration)

carbohydrates_pct.method: Total sugars after acid hydrolysis (stated for illustration)

data_gaps.impact: Every figure in this profile is invented for demonstration. Results based on it say nothing about a real mill.
data_gaps.next_step: Replace the profile with the mill's own lab data and production records.

data_gaps.next_step: Request an inorganic element analysis of the ash.

data_gaps.next_step: Confirm the analytical method with the lab and use the same one when comparing with buyers' specifications.

checks.disclaimer: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.

current_use.description: Fictional: the precipitated lignin is fired in the mill's own boilers in place of purchased fuel. The unit was built to relieve the recovery boiler, not to sell lignin.

geographic_market.logistics: Fictional: rail siding at the mill; the nearest deep-water port is assumed to be about 150 km away.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.feedstock:constraints[3]: "Chemical modification equipment is not available, limiting pathways that require modified lignin."
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#1: UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins used for wood-panel adhesives, with typical replacement up to 50% after activation or depolymerization.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin is reported for veneer plywood, including industrially proven resin meeting EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3.
A laboratory study used depolymerized kraft lignin as 50% of the phenolic component in plywood resin that met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in that study.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include plywood producers and other wood-based-panel adhesive or resin manufacturers.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is phenol used in phenol-formaldehyde resins.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before use in the PF-resin route described by the evidence.
For veneer plywood, the cited LPF resin meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3; formaldehyde emissions were measured under EN 717-2.
The cited laboratory formulation used 50% depolymerized lignin in the phenolic component and evaluated viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde against a Chinese wood-adhesive standard.
The fictional stream lacks chemical-modification equipment, so a buyer or partner would need to provide the activation or depolymerization step.

limitations: The strongest commercial evidence is vendor technical literature from UPM, and its document does not state that the lignin is kraft lignin or provide composition.

The reported TRL 8 applies to biobased phenolic resins generally, while TRL 9 applies to a LignoBoost extraction plus resin-substitution configuration; neither establishes commercial readiness for this specific wet stream.
The laboratory plywood study used poplar samples and reports an inconsistency in the cited Chinese standard.
The evidence does not establish performance using this fictional stream's unmeasured ash, molecular weight, or phenolic hydroxyl content.
missing_information: No current lignin selling price, purchase volume, named buyer, contract terms, or regional demand estimate is provided.
No evidence quantifies the cost of drying or pretreating this wet-cake stream.
No evidence confirms that the stream meets the resin process's molecular-weight or composition conditions.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence includes documented industrially proven LPF resin from a lignin producer and a claim of meeting a plywood bonding class, which supports the rubric's level for documented commercial sales by at least one lignin producer. The broader technical evidence is supplemented by laboratory and review results rather than several established buyers.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#2: In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#2: Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.feedstock:constraints[3]: "Chemical modification equipment is not available, limiting pathways that require modified lignin."
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Unmodified lignin has been tested as a partial replacement for petroleum-based polyol in rigid polyurethane and polyisocyanurate insulation foams.

Unmodified lignin has also been tested as a partial replacement for petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam; kraft lignins produced denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.

The evidence describes polyurethane uses including foams, panels, coatings, and rubber replacement, with kraft lignin replacement reported after oxypropylation, depolymerization and oxypropylation, or liquefaction in a bio-based polyol.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include rigid insulation-foam producers, flexible-foam producers, and manufacturers of polyurethane panels, coatings, or rubber-replacement materials.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is petroleum-based polyol.

qualification_requirements.statement: For rigid polyurethane foam, the cited acceptable range is total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g, equivalent to 3.56 mmol/g total hydroxyl groups; this is not a phenolic-hydroxyl requirement.
The cited rigid PUR/PIR qualification used ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications, including compressive strength and closed-cell content requirements.
Kraft lignin generally needs significant treatment such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction to reach target polyurethane properties.
The fictional stream lacks chemical-modification equipment, so modified-lignin polyurethane routes would require external processing by a buyer or partner.

limitations: Most evidence is laboratory foam work, and the reported results vary by lignin type, formulation, and substitution basis.
The cited TRL 6 applies to a broad polyurethane category rather than specifically to kraft-lignin foam production.
A review says commercialization remains limited by product consistency, technical performance, and production costs, and the full text was unavailable.
Some softwood kraft lignins may have sulfur odor, while odor was not measured in the cited flexible-foam study.
missing_information: No current lignin price, polyurethane-grade contract volume, named buyer, or regional demand estimate is provided.
No evidence demonstrates qualification of this fictional stream in a commercial foam, panel, coating, or rubber application.
The stream's total hydroxyl value, ash, molecular weight, moisture, and other composition properties are not available.
No evidence quantifies the cost or feasibility of required lignin modification for this mill.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence shows research-scale testing and a broad TRL 6 assessment, but it also states that commercialization remains limited and provides no documented commercial lignin sales to polyurethane buyers. This fits the rubric's research-literature or announcement level rather than documented industry trials or commercial sales.

supported_claims.EV-CM-02#3: Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#4: Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#1: DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#3: Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
supported_claims.feedstock:constraints[5]: "Ash is missing, and sodium is missing, so inorganic-content requirements cannot be fully assessed."
supported_claims.feedstock:constraints[2]: "Solvent or membrane fractionation is not available, limiting pathways that require fractionated lignin."
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).

applications.statement: Softwood lignin has been investigated as a precursor for carbon fiber, but it is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent and the cited lignin-based fibers reached about 50% of the mechanical-property target in that work.

Kraft lignin can be used as a precursor for hard carbon for sodium-ion battery anodes; a review reports higher initial coulombic efficiency for hard carbon from kraft lignin than from sulfonated lignin in the cited comparison.
Lignin can be converted into activated carbon, including when its precursor quality is too poor for other carbon-material uses.
Lignin-based hard carbon has also been developed for lithium-ion battery anode material, with a reported pilot production line and planned scale-up in standardized manufacturing units.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include carbon-fiber producers, sodium-ion battery-anode developers, lithium-ion battery manufacturers, and activated-carbon producers.

competing_materials.statement: The cited carbon-fiber incumbent is PAN-based carbon fiber.
For sodium-ion battery hard carbon, the evidence compares lignin with anthracite and cellulose feedstocks.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited carbon-fiber precursor specification requires lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
Kraft lignin examined for carbon fiber needed purification, and softwood lignin needed a plasticizing or alloying agent for melt spinning.
Lower ash improves activated-carbon yield, although activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality in the cited study.
The fictional stream's ash and sodium are missing, so inorganic-content suitability cannot be fully assessed; its lack of fractionation capability also limits routes requiring fractionated lignin.

limitations: Carbon fiber, hard carbon, and activated carbon have materially different quality requirements, so evidence for one product cannot be generalized to the others.
The carbon-fiber specifications are cited secondhand, and the study's lignin came from a near-neutral hemicellulose extraction process rather than standard kraft pulping.
The GreenLight evidence reports TRL 5 for precursor-fiber production, not the complete lignin-to-carbon-fiber chain, and its costs are modelled rather than measured.
The battery evidence includes reviews and company investor material; the latter contains forward-looking statements and its later status was not verified.
The activated-carbon evidence is laboratory work using zinc chloride activation.
missing_information: No current selling price, purchase volume, named buyer, contract terms, or regional demand estimate is provided for any of the three carbon-material submarkets.
No evidence confirms that this stream meets carbon-fiber precursor specifications, especially ash, lignin purity, volatiles, residual carbohydrates, particulates, or melt-spinnability.
No product-specific qualification pathway or customer acceptance data is provided for hard carbon or activated carbon from this stream.
No evidence quantifies drying, purification, activation, carbonization, or spinning costs for the fictional wet cake.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents development partnerships and pilot activity, including GreenLight precursor-fiber production at TRL 5 and a reported battery-anode pilot line, but it does not establish commercial sales by several lignin producers or established buyers. This supports the rubric's documented trials, pilots, or development-partnership level.

processing_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin would need activation or depolymerization before use in the PF-resin route.
Because the mill has no chemical-modification equipment, activation or depolymerization would need to be supplied by a buyer or external partner.

A downstream customer would need to qualify the resin for panel-adhesive performance, including the relevant bonding, formaldehyde-emissions, viscosity, bonding-strength, and free-formaldehyde requirements.

technical_maturity.statement: The resin route is assessed at TRL 9, which maps to the highest technical-readiness score.

adoption_barriers.statement: The route competes with phenol and requires customers such as plywood or wood-panel resin producers to accept a qualified lignin-containing formulation.
The fictional stream has not been shown to meet the route's molecular-weight or composition conditions, and key composition properties are missing.
Wet-cake handling and the absence of a mill dryer create a drying requirement for buyers needing dry powder, while external sales compete with the lignin's current boiler-fuel use.

missing_inputs: confirmation that the stream meets resin molecular-weight or composition conditions
assumptions: The economics tool used fictional wet-feedstock masses of 36000.0 / 40000.0 / 43000.0 t/yr for the conservative / base / optimistic cases.
The economics tool used fictional moisture assumptions of 40.0 / 35.0 / 30.0% of wet mass for the conservative / base / optimistic cases.
The economics tool used fictional availability fractions of 40.0 / 50.0 / 60.0% for the conservative / base / optimistic cases.
The economics tool calculated dry mass and usable dry feedstock, but assumed no default product yield, price, or variable cost.
Commercialization assumes a buyer or partner can provide activation or depolymerization and downstream resin qualification.
uncertainties: Product output, revenue, variable cost, gross contribution, contribution per tonne, and indicative economics score were not calculated because product yield, product price, and variable costs are missing.
Moisture is uncertain and affects dry tonnage and shipped mass.
The commercial opportunity is not validated by a named buyer, price, contract, or regional demand estimate.
The feedstock's ash, molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl, and sodium properties remain unconfirmed.
The TRL evidence describes a resin technology route, but does not establish qualification of this specific wet-cake stream.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: The route is technically mature and has identifiable panel-resin customers, but commercialization for this mill requires significant external processing and qualification because activation or depolymerization equipment is absent and feedstock suitability is not confirmed.

feedstock_compatibility.rationale: The evidence library has no numeric requirements for this pathway to check against.

technical_readiness.rationale: TRL 9 maps to 5. Stated in EV-PF-03#1.

ranking_changers: A complete dry-basis economics comparison—especially yield, selling price, variable costs, drying cost, external processing cost, and the value of displaced boiler fuel—could reorder the pathways because indicative economics is currently unassessed for all three.

Phenolic-resin compatibility and process-trial results could move that pathway from insufficient data into the leading position, consistent with its high provisional attractiveness and TRL 9 evidence.

Carbon-material qualification could either strengthen the current rank-one position or substantially reduce it if the carbon-fiber checks fail and no hard-carbon or activated-carbon route is demonstrated.
A successful polyurethane qualification with measured total hydroxyl value, modification economics, and a named buyer could lift the currently lowest provisional pathway.
caveats: The feedstock stream and its stated annual dry mass are fictional; moisture is uncertain, so shipped wet mass and usable dry tonnage are unresolved.
The ranking follows the deterministic scoring engine. Phenolic resins and polyurethanes are listed as insufficient data rather than ranked because only 0.55 of the criterion weight was assessed.

Carbon-material compatibility is based on checked carbon-fiber requirements and does not establish suitability for every hard-carbon or activated-carbon submarket.
The assessment does not quantify the opportunity cost of continuing to fire lignin in the mill boilers.
report.summary: Carbon materials is the only pathway currently ranked, at rank 1, because it has the highest assessed compatibility contribution and documented pilot/development evidence, although its economics is unassessed and commercialization feasibility is low. Phenolic resins has the strongest provisional attractiveness and the clearest maturity and market evidence, but missing compatibility and economics data prevent a formal rank. Polyurethanes trails on market evidence and feasibility and also lacks compatibility and economics data. The next decision should prioritize feedstock characterization, external conversion trials, buyer qualification, and a dry-basis contribution model.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.
Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
A techno-economic comparison lists LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins ('LB+Resin') at TRL 9.
